sports-court-size-guide: Choose badminton, tennis, pickleball, basketball, volleyball, football, cricket, hockey, kabaddi, kho kho, table tennis or squash. Then choose the version, such as doubles or 3x3, or the pitch size.
Read the size and the space needed
The court is drawn to scale. Sizes are in metres with feet and inches in brackets, and the space needed includes the clear space around the court that the rules ask for.
Mark the outer rectangle, check that both diagonals match, then measure the key lines from the distances listed.
Enter the length and width of your hall, ground or plot. The guide lists which courts fit, how many, and how much room is spare or missing.
Each sport lists notes, risks, how to play it, its playing rules, the sources used and the date they were checked. Confirm with the governing body before you build.
cricket-run-rate-calculator: Pick Run chase for the required run rate, Net run rate for a tournament table or Player stats for averages and strike rates.
Select 5, 8, 10, 15, 20, 30 or 50 overs, which sets how many balls each team has.
Type runs and overs as cricketers write them, so 18.4 means 18 overs and 4 balls. Tick the boxes if a team was bowled out.
See the rates at once, and copy the summary to share in a match chat.
match-score-keeper: Choose badminton, tennis, volleyball, table tennis, squash or pickleball, then choose a single game or best of 3, 5 or 7 where it applies.
Type the player or team names over Player 1 and Player 2.
Press the big button under the side that won the rally. The tool follows the rules for games, sets, deuce, tie-breaks and winning by two.
Use Undo last point if you tapped the wrong side. The tool reminds you to change ends and shows the winner of the match.
tournament-fixtures-maker: Type one team or player on each line, up to 32. For a knockout, put the strongest first.
Pick round robin where everyone plays once, home and away where everyone plays twice, or a knockout bracket.
In a round robin, type the score of each match. In a knockout, tap the winner of each match.
Read the points table or the champion, and copy the fixtures to send to the group.
cricket-scorer: Open the page and you are on the first ball. There are no teams, names or overs to set up.
Tap 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6 for runs, or Wicket. For a wide, no-ball, bye or leg bye, pick that button first, then tap the runs.

The score, wickets, overs, run rate, balls of this over, extras, fours and sixes and the partnership update after every ball. Open Over by over to see the runs and balls of every earlier over. It stays closed until you open it.
Tap Undo last ball if you made a mistake. Under Options you can set the overs, set a target for a chase or start the chase after the first innings.
quick-scoreboard: Pick basketball, football, hockey, kabaddi, handball or any other game. The buttons change to suit the game.
Type over Home and Away to give each side its name.
Tap +1, +2 or +3 under the side that scored. In basketball you can also count fouls for each side.
Start the clock, pick the period or half from the list, and tap Undo for a mistake. Show it on a big screen for the crowd.
kho-kho-court-size: The drawing below is to scale, with the 27 m x 16 m size written on it in metres and feet. Use Save as image or Save as PDF to take the marking plan to the ground.
Measure 27 m for the long sides and 16 m for the ends, and put a peg at each corner. Check that both diagonals are 31.38 m, which shows the corners are square.
Mark the central lane 0.3 m wide and the 8 cross lanes 0.35 m wide each. Fix the two poles 1.2 m high, which is the lower value of the 120 to 125 cm range.
Confirm the size and the number of players with the rules of your event or the Kho Kho Federation of India before a match, because school and local grounds often differ.
kabaddi-court-size: Pick the men and junior boys court (13 m x 10 m), the women and junior girls court (12 m x 8 m) or the sub-junior court (11 m x 8 m) in the Version box.
Measure the length and width, put a peg at each corner and check that both diagonals match: 16.4 m for the men's court, 14.42 m for the women's court and 13.6 m for the sub-junior court.
Mark the midline, then a baulk line on each side of it and a bonus line 1 m beyond each baulk line. The numbers for your version are in the marking plan below.
Mark a 1 m strip along both long sides for the lobbies, then confirm the size with your state association or the IKF rules for your event.
badminton-court-size: The drawing is to scale with the length and width written on it in metres and feet. The court is 13.4 m x 6.1 m for doubles, and singles uses the same court with the inner side lines.
Measure 13.4 m for the long sides and 6.1 m for the ends and peg the four corners. Check that both diagonals are 14.72 m, which shows the corners are square.
Add the service lines and net

Mark the net line 6.7 m from each back line, the short service line 1.98 m from the net, the long service line for doubles 0.76 m in from the back line, the centre line 3.05 m from the side and the singles side lines 0.46 m inside the outer lines.
Check the space and the rules
Plan 2 m clear behind the back lines and 1.5 m at the sides for competition, then confirm with your federation. Save the marking plan as an image or PDF to take to the hall.
tennis-court-size: The drawing is to scale with the sizes in metres and feet. A tennis court is 23.77 m x 10.97 m for doubles, and singles uses the inner side lines 8.23 m apart.
Measure 23.77 m for the sides and 10.97 m for the baselines and peg the corners. Check that both diagonals are 26.18 m, which shows the corners are square.
Add the net, service lines and centre line
Mark the net 11.885 m from each baseline, the service lines 6.4 m from the net, the centre service line down the middle and the singles side lines 1.37 m inside the doubles lines.
Plan 5.48 m behind the baselines and 3.05 m at the sides for club play, or 6.4 m and 3.66 m for international play, then save the marking plan as an image or PDF.
pickleball-court-size: The drawing is to scale. A pickleball court is 13.41 m x 6.096 m (44 ft x 20 ft), the same for singles and doubles, which is the size of a doubles badminton court.
Measure 13.41 m for the sides and 6.096 m for the ends and peg the corners. Check that both diagonals are 14.73 m, which shows the corners are square.
Add the net, kitchen and centre lines
Mark the net across the middle, 6.706 m from each end line. Mark the kitchen line 2.134 m (7 ft) from the net on each side, and the centre line down the middle of each half behind the kitchen.
Plan a playing area of at least 9.14 m x 18.29 m (30 ft x 60 ft), or 10.36 m x 19.51 m (34 ft x 64 ft) for tournaments, then save the marking plan.
basketball-court-size: Choose the FIBA full court (28 m x 15 m) or the 3x3 court (15 m x 11 m) in the Version box. The drawing is to scale with the sizes written on it in metres and feet.
For a full court, measure 28 m by 15 m and peg the corners. Check that both diagonals are 31.76 m. For 3x3, measure 15 m by 11 m and check that both diagonals are 18.6 m.

On a full court, mark the halfway line 14 m from each end, the free-throw line 5.8 m from each end line, the lane 4.9 m wide, the three-point corner lines 0.9 m in from the side lines and the centre circle with a radius of 1.8 m.
Check the space and the rules
Keep obstructions at least 2 m from the court and confirm the size with FIBA or your league, then save the marking plan as an image or PDF.
volleyball-court-size: Choose the indoor court (18 m x 9 m) or the beach court (16 m x 8 m) in the Version box. The drawing is to scale with the sizes in metres and feet.
For indoor, measure 18 m by 9 m and check that both diagonals are 20.12 m. For beach, measure 16 m by 8 m and check that both diagonals are 17.89 m.
Add the centre and attack lines
Mark the centre line under the net, at 9 m from each end line for indoor. Mark each attack line 3 m from the centre line, which is 6 m from the end line.
Set the net and the free zone
Net height is 2.43 m for men and 2.24 m for women. Plan at least 3 m of clear space on all sides, or 8 m at the ends and 5 m at the sides for official events.
football-pitch-size: The Laws allow 90 to 120 m in length and 45 to 90 m in width. Pick the smallest, the smallest international size, the common 105 m x 68 m or the largest in the Version box.
Measure the touchlines and goal lines and peg the corners. For 105 m x 68 m, check that both diagonals are 125.1 m, which shows the corners are square.
Add the halfway line and circle
Mark the halfway line across the middle and the centre circle with a radius of 9.15 m around the centre spot.
Mark the goal and penalty areas
Mark each goal area 5.5 m from the goal line, each penalty area 16.5 m from it, the penalty mark 11 m from the goal line and the corner arcs with a radius of 1 m.
cricket-pitch-size: A cricket pitch is 22 yards (20.12 m) long and 10 ft (3.05 m) wide. Choose Pitch only in the Version box to see it to scale.
Peg a rectangle 20.12 m by 3.048 m and check that both diagonals are 20.35 m. Mark the centre line 1.524 m (5 ft) from each side.
Choose a boundary in the Version box. Men's international boundaries are 65 to 90 yards from the centre of the pitch, and women's international boundaries are 60 to 70 yards.
For limited-overs matches, mark a fielding circle with a radius of 27.43 m (30 yards) from each wicket, and keep boards and fencing at least 3 yards (2.74 m) outside the boundary.
hockey-pitch-size: A field hockey pitch is 91.4 m (100 yards) long and 55 m (60 yards) wide. The drawing is to scale with the sizes written on it in metres and feet.
Measure 91.4 m for the side lines and 55 m for the back lines and peg the corners. Check that both diagonals are 106.67 m, which shows the corners are square.
Mark the halfway line 45.7 m from each back line, the 23 m lines 22.9 m from each back line and the shooting circle with a radius of 14.63 m at each end.
Each goal is 3.66 m wide and 2.14 m high, outside the back line. Mark the penalty spot 6.475 m from the goal line and keep 3 m of run-off behind the back lines.
table-tennis-table-size: A table tennis table is 2.74 m x 1.525 m and 0.76 m high. Choose The table in the Version box to see it to scale with the net line.
The net is 15.25 cm (6 in) high above the playing surface and sits across the middle, 1.37 m from each end.
Choose a space in the Version box: competition 14 m x 7 m, masters 10 m x 5 m or wheelchair events 8 m x 6 m. Competition needs 5 m of height.
Leave enough room to step back from the table, then use Fit my space on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to check a room, and save the drawing as an image or PDF.
squash-court-size: Choose the singles court (9.75 m x 6.4 m) or the doubles court (13.72 m x 7.62 m) in the Version box. The drawing is to scale in metres and feet.
On a singles court the front wall top line is 4.57 m high and the back wall top line is 2.13 m high. A doubles court has a front wall top line of 6.09 m.

The tin is 0.48 m high, and the service line on the front wall is 1.78 m high. Heights are measured on the walls and are not floor distances.

sportsCourtGuide.title: Sports Court and Ground Size Guide: Dimensions and Fit My Space
sportsCourtGuide.subtitle: Court and ground sizes for 13 sports to scale in metres and feet, with a marking plan, how to play and the playing rules for each sport. Free and private.
faq: What is the size of a badminton court?

A badminton court is 13.4 m (44 ft) long and 6.1 m (20 ft) wide for doubles. For singles the court is 5.18 m wide, using the inner side lines. The BWF asks for about 2 m behind the back lines and 1.5 m at the sides in competition halls.
How big is a tennis court?
A tennis court is 23.77 m (78 ft) long and 10.97 m (36 ft) wide for doubles, and 8.23 m (27 ft) wide for singles. The ITF recommends 5.48 m behind the baselines and 3.05 m at the sides for club play.
What size is a pickleball court?
A pickleball court is 6.1 m x 13.41 m (20 ft x 44 ft), the same for singles and doubles, with a 2.13 m (7 ft) non-volley zone on each side of the net.
How long is a cricket pitch?
The pitch is 22 yards (20.12 m) long and 10 ft (3.05 m) wide. The size of the ground is not fixed; international boundaries for men are between 65 and 90 yards from the centre of the pitch.
Does football have one fixed pitch size?
No. The Laws of the Game allow 90 to 120 m in length and 45 to 90 m in width, and 100 to 110 m by 64 to 75 m for international matches. 105 m x 68 m is common but is not a rule.
How does Fit my space work?

You enter the length and width of your space and any extra clear space you want. The guide adds the clear space the rules ask for around each court and lists which courts fit, how many fit side by side, and the spare room or the shortfall.
Are these sizes official?

They come from the governing bodies or sources listed on each sport, and the check date is shown. Some figures come from summaries of the rules or older editions, and the notes say so. Rules change, so confirm with the federation for your event.
Can I use this to build or mark a court?
It is a planning guide. Use it to plan and to mark lines, but confirm the rules for your event and have a qualified person check the safety and surface of a venue before you build.
Why do school and local courts differ from these sizes?
Recreational, school and club courts are often smaller than the full sizes, and some leagues set their own limits. Follow the rulebook of your league or federation.

sportsCricketRunRate.title: Cricket Run Rate Calculator: Required Rate, Net Run Rate and Averages
sportsCricketRunRate.subtitle: Required run rate in a chase, net run rate across a tournament, plus batting average, strike rate, economy and bowling average. Free cricket calculator.
faq: How is net run rate calculated?

Net run rate is the runs a team scores per over across all its matches, minus the runs it concedes per over. A team that scored 340 runs in 40 overs and conceded 320 in 40 overs has a rate of 8.5 minus 8.0, which is plus 0.5.
How are overs written?

Cricketers write overs as whole overs, a dot and the balls, so 18.4 is 18 overs and 4 balls, which is 112 balls. The tool accepts that form and rejects anything above 5 balls after the dot. It then uses the real number of balls in the sums, because 18.4 overs is not 18.4 in decimal.
What happens when a team is bowled out?
In net run rate calculations a team that is bowled out is counted as having faced its full quota of overs, not the overs it lasted. Tick the bowled out box and the tool does this for you.
How is the required run rate worked out?

It is the runs still needed divided by the balls left, multiplied by six. If a team needs 80 runs from 60 balls, the required rate is 8.00 runs an over. The tool also shows the current run rate and the score at that rate.
Does it handle rain-affected matches?
Not automatically. Tournaments use different rules, such as a revised target or a reduced quota of overs. If a match was shortened, enter the official revised figures for it.
What do the player stats mean?

Batting average is runs divided by times out, and strike rate is runs per 100 balls. Economy is runs conceded per over, bowling average is runs conceded per wicket and balls per wicket is the bowling strike rate.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?
No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. Your scores are used only in the page. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

sportsMatchScoreKeeper.title: Match Score Keeper: Badminton, Tennis, Volleyball and Table Tennis Scoreboard
sportsMatchScoreKeeper.subtitle: Keep the score of badminton, tennis, volleyball, table tennis, squash or pickleball with big buttons, undo and the right rules. Free, saved on your device.
faq: Which sports can it score?
Badminton, tennis, volleyball, table tennis, squash and pickleball with rally scoring. Each uses its own rules for points per game, winning by two, and the number of games or sets.
How does tennis scoring work here?

Points go 15, 30, 40 and game, with deuce and advantage at 40 all. A set is won at 6 games with a lead of two, and a tie-break to 7 points is played at 6-6. Matches are a single set or best of 3 or 5.
What if I tap the wrong side?
Press Undo last point. It takes back one point at a time, as far back as the start of the match, and every score is recalculated.
Does it tell me when to change ends?

It shows a reminder, for example in the deciding game of badminton when a side reaches 11, in table tennis at 5 in the last game, after each volleyball set and after odd games in tennis. Always follow your umpire or event rules.
Does it track who is serving?
No. It keeps the score only, so the serve is still tracked by the players or the umpire.
Will I lose the score if I close the page?
No. The score is saved on your device, so it is there when you come back. Press New match to start again.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. The score and names are saved only in this browser. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

sportsTournamentFixtures.title: Tournament Fixtures Maker: Round Robin, Knockout Bracket and Points Table
sportsTournamentFixtures.subtitle: Make fixtures for a round robin, home and away or knockout tournament, enter scores for a live points table and copy the schedule. Free, no sign-up.
faq: What is a round robin?
A round robin is a tournament where every team plays every other team once. The tool lists the matches in rounds so that no team plays twice in the same round, and each team plays all the others.
How are byes handled?
With an odd number of teams in a round robin, one team rests in each round. In a knockout, if the number of teams is not 2, 4, 8, 16 or 32, the top seeds get a bye and go straight to the next round.
How does the points table work?
Each match gives points for a win, a draw or a loss. You can change the points for a win and a draw. Teams are ordered by points, then score difference, then scores for, and then by name.
How are knockout matches seeded?
Teams are placed so that the top seeds meet as late as possible. With 8 teams, seed 1 plays seed 8, 4 plays 5, 2 plays 7 and 3 plays 6. The order of your list is the seeding.
Can I save and share the fixtures?
The tool keeps your teams and results on this device. Use Copy the fixtures to paste the schedule into a chat or document. Clear all results starts again with the same teams.
Is there a limit on teams?
Up to 32 teams. For very large tournaments, split the teams into groups and make one fixture list for each.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. Your teams and results are saved only in this browser. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

sportsCricketScorer.title: Cricket Scorer: Ball by Ball Scoreboard with Run Rate, Free Hit and Undo
sportsCricketScorer.subtitle: Score a cricket innings ball by ball with no setup. Tap runs, wickets, wides and no-balls to see the score, overs, run rate and partnership. Free, no sign-up.
faq: Do I need to set up teams, players or overs?
No. Open the page and start tapping the result of each ball. Overs, a target and a chase are optional and sit under Options, so a game in the street needs nothing at all.
How are wides and no-balls counted?

A wide or a no-ball adds 1 run to the total and the ball is not counted, so the over lasts until six fair balls have been bowled. Pick Wide or No-ball first, then tap 0 or the extra runs. After a no-ball the screen shows a free hit.
How do byes and leg byes work?
Pick Bye or Leg bye, then tap the runs. The runs go to extras and the ball counts as a fair ball.
What does the partnership show?
It shows the runs, and the number of balls in brackets, scored since the last wicket fell.
Can I score a chase?

Yes. Under Options set a target and the overs and the screen shows the runs needed, the balls left and the required run rate. You can also tap End innings and start the chase to take the first innings score plus one as the target.
Can I show the score on a bigger screen?

Yes. Tap Show on a big screen to fill the display with the score. It is available on computers, tablets and many phones, but not on the iPhone, where you can turn the phone sideways or cast the page instead.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?

No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. The innings is saved only in this browser, so it is still here if you close the page. Tap New match to clear it. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

sportsQuickScoreboard.title: Quick Scoreboard: Basketball, Football, Hockey and Kabaddi Score Counter
sportsQuickScoreboard.subtitle: A simple scoreboard for basketball, football, hockey, kabaddi, handball or any game, with big score buttons, fouls, a clock and undo. Free, no sign-up.
faq: Which games does it support?
Basketball, football, hockey, kabaddi and handball have their own buttons and periods. Any other game gives you +1, +2, +3 and +5 buttons, so it works for almost anything.
What do the buttons add?

Basketball has +1 for a free throw, +2 for a shot and +3 for a shot from outside the arc. Football, hockey and handball have +1 for a goal. Kabaddi has +1 for a point and +2 for an All Out or a super tackle.
Does it keep time?

It has a simple clock that you start and pause by hand, and a list of periods such as quarters or halves. It counts up and does not stop or ring by itself, so use it as a guide and follow the official timekeeper.
What if I add a score by mistake?
Tap Undo last score. It removes one score at a time, as far back as the start of the game.
Can I show it to a crowd?
Yes. Tap Show on a big screen to fill the display with the scores and the clock. It works on computers, tablets and most Android phones, but not on the iPhone, where you can cast the page instead.
Is the score saved?
The score, names, fouls and the clock are saved on your device, so they are still here if you close the page. Tap New game to clear them.
Is anything I enter uploaded or stored?
No. Everything runs in your browser and nothing you enter is sent to {{siteName}}. Nothing is saved anywhere else. The page still loads fonts, advertising and other resources from the network.

sportsKhoKhoCourt.title: Kho Kho Court Size: Ground Measurements and Marking Plan
sportsKhoKhoCourt.subtitle: Kho kho ground size in metres and feet, drawn to scale, with lane widths, pole height, a marking plan, how to play and the playing rules. Free and private.
faq: What is the size of a kho kho ground?
A kho kho ground is a rectangle 27 m long and 16 m wide, which is 88 ft 7 in by 52 ft 5.9 in. The guide uses the sizes published at khokho.net, and the date they were checked is shown on the page.
How wide are the central lane and the cross lanes?

The central lane is 0.3 m (11.8 in) wide and each of the 8 cross lanes is 0.35 m (1 ft 1.8 in) wide. The source we used gives the number and width of the cross lanes, but not the spacing between them, so the drawing shows only the outer rectangle.
How high are the kho kho poles?
The poles are 120 to 125 cm high. The guide shows the lower value, 1.2 m (3 ft 11.2 in).
How do I mark a kho kho ground on grass or a playground?

Peg out a 27 m by 16 m rectangle and check that both diagonals measure 31.38 m. Equal diagonals show the corners are square. Then mark the central lane and cross lanes. The marking plan on this page can be saved as an image or a PDF.
How many players are in a kho kho team?
The guide describes nine players in a team, with three runners on the ground at a time. Some events, such as the World Cup, use seven a side, so check the rules of your event.
How long is a kho kho match?

sections.heading: Why court sizes are worth checking
paragraphs: Most sports are played on a marked area whose length, width and lines are fixed by a governing body. The numbers are easy to mix up: a doubles court is wider than a singles court, a hall needs clear space beyond the lines, and a ground may be allowed to vary within a range.
This guide puts the main sizes for 13 sports in one place, drawn to scale. Every length is shown in metres with feet and inches in brackets, so it works whether your tape measure is metric or not.

sections.heading: What each sport page shows
paragraphs: Each page shows the court drawn to scale, the main measurements, the clear space around the court and the overall space needed. A marking plan lists the distances to mark the lines and the diagonal that must be equal to show the corners are square.
A short how-to-play section gives the aim, scoring and key rules in plain words, and the notes list things to watch out for. The sources and the date they were checked are shown at the bottom.

sections.heading: Fit my space
paragraphs: If you already have a hall, a garden or a plot, enter its length and width. The guide adds the clear space each court needs, tries the courts both ways round and lists which of them fit, how many fit and how much room is spare or missing. You can add extra clear space if you want a bigger safety gap than the rules ask for.

sections.heading: Limits and risks
paragraphs: Sizes come from the sources listed and were checked on the date shown. Some come from summaries of the rules or older editions, such as the volleyball clear space, the cricket boundary limits and the hockey figures, and the notes on each page say so.

Football has no run-off distance in the Laws, and table tennis has an official size only for competition. Cricket grounds are oval but are drawn and counted as circles. Kho kho lane positions and cricket creases are not drawn. Always confirm with your federation, and have the surface, height and safety of a venue checked by a qualified person.

sections.heading: Why run rates matter
paragraphs: Run rates tell you how fast runs are coming, which is the heart of limited-overs cricket. In a chase the required rate shows how hard the job is, and in a tournament table the net run rate separates teams that finish on the same points.

Computing them by hand is slow and easy to get wrong, especially when overs are written as 18.4 or when a team is bowled out. This tool does the sums for you and shows the figures a captain or scorer needs.

sections.heading: Net run rate across a tournament
paragraphs: To find the net run rate, add up all the runs a team has scored and all the overs it has faced, then do the same for the runs it has conceded and the overs it has bowled. Divide each pair, and subtract the second rate from the first. The tool lets you add a match at a time, with up to twelve matches, and keeps the running figure.

If a side is bowled out, the full quota of overs is counted, which stops a team from gaining by being bowled out cheaply and quickly. Rain-reduced games follow the rules of each tournament, so enter their official figures.

sections.heading: Averages and strike rates
paragraphs: Player stats help compare batters and bowlers who have played different numbers of matches. A batting average shows how many runs a batter makes for each time they are out, while the strike rate shows how fast they score. For bowlers, economy shows how many runs they give away in an over, and bowling average and balls per wicket show how often they take wickets.

These numbers are a summary and do not replace watching the game. A batter with a low average might have been given a difficult role, and a bowler with a high economy might have been bowling in the closing overs.

sections.heading: A scoreboard for any court
paragraphs: A friendly match still needs a score everyone agrees on. This keeper has two big buttons that are easy to press on a phone, even with sweaty hands, and a large score that can be read across the court. Rules are built in, so you do not argue about whether a game ends at 21 or needs a two-point lead.

It works for casual play, club nights, school sports days and coaching. Because it runs in the browser there is nothing to install, and the score is saved on the device so a lost signal or a closed tab does not wipe the match.

sections.heading: How the rules are applied
paragraphs: In badminton a game goes to 21 with a lead of two and stops at 30, and a match is the best of three games. Table tennis games go to 11, squash to 11, pickleball to 11 with rally scoring, and volleyball to 25, with a deciding set to 15, all with a two-point lead needed. Tennis follows the 15, 30, 40 pattern with deuce and a tie-break at 6-6 in every set.
Rules differ between events and age groups. If your competition uses another format, such as games to 15, use the tool for the score and the official rules for the result.

sections.heading: Getting the most from it
paragraphs: Set the names first so everyone can see who is who. Press the button as soon as a rally ends, and use Undo if you press the wrong one. Watch the hint line for ends changes, and look at the finished games line to see how earlier games went.
Put a phone or tablet where the players can see it, or cast it to a bigger screen for a club match. The Sports Court Guide has the playing rules for each sport if you need to check a decision.

sections.heading: Fixtures without the headache
paragraphs: Planning who plays whom is easy for four teams and painful for eleven. The circle method used here arranges every team against every other team with the fewest rounds, and keeps the home and away spots balanced. You type the names and the list is ready in a second.
For a knockout, the tool seeds the bracket so that the strongest teams are kept apart until the later rounds, and it gives byes when the number of teams is not a power of two.

sections.heading: Points tables and brackets
paragraphs: As results come in, type the score of each match and the table updates. Teams are ordered by points, then score difference, then scores for. Change the points for a win and a draw to match your league, for example 2 for a win in some leagues and 3 in others.
In a knockout, just tap the winner of each match and the bracket fills in, round by round, up to the final and the champion.

sections.heading: Running a tournament well
paragraphs: Tell everyone the format and the tie-break rules before the first match, and keep the points table visible. If you are short of courts or time, a single round robin in groups followed by a short knockout is a good way to give every team several matches.
Use the Match Score Keeper for the scores of individual matches, and the Sports Court Guide to mark out the court you need.

sections.heading: Scoring with no setup
paragraphs: A full scorecard needs two teams, eleven names each, an overs limit and a lot of patience. Most games, from a gully match to a society tournament, only need the score. This scorer opens ready to go: tap what happened on each ball and the numbers keep up.
There is nothing to configure and nothing to sign in to. The innings is saved on your phone as you go, so a closed tab or a dead battery in the browser does not lose the match.

sections.heading: What it works out for you
paragraphs: From the list of balls the scorer works out the total, the wickets, the overs written the cricket way, the run rate, the extras, the fours and sixes, the balls of the current over and the partnership since the last wicket. The Over by over list, which is closed until you open it, shows each over's balls, runs, wickets and the total at its end. If you set the overs it shows how many are left and the score you are on course for at the current rate.
In a chase it shows the runs needed, the balls left and the required run rate, and tells you when the target has been reached.

sections.heading: Getting it right on the field
paragraphs: Choose the kind of ball before the runs, so a no-ball that went for four is No-ball then 4. Wides and no-balls do not count as a ball, which is why the over counter does not move. If you tap the wrong button, Undo takes back one ball at a time.
Local rules differ, especially in street cricket, so agree beforehand whether a wide or a no-ball counts a run. This scorer follows the standard rule of one run for each.

sections.heading: A scoreboard in one tap
paragraphs: For a school match, a tournament day or a game in the park you often just need two big numbers that everybody can see. This scoreboard has them. Pick the game, tap the big button under the side that scored, and the score changes at once.

Basketball gets a three-point button and a foul counter for each side, kabaddi gets a two-point button for an All Out, and a plain +1 does for football, hockey and handball. Any other game gets +1, +2, +3 and +5.

sections.heading: Clock, periods and undo
paragraphs: A start and pause clock counts up from zero, and a list of periods lets you mark quarters, halves or rounds. The clock is a helper for the scorer and does not replace the official timekeeper, because it does not stop at the end of a period by itself.
Every score is stored as a list, so Undo removes the last one and the total is worked out again. That makes it safe to tap fast during a busy moment and fix a slip afterwards.

sections.heading: Showing it to the crowd
paragraphs: Tap Show on a big screen to fill the display with the scores, the period and the clock. Put a tablet or a laptop on a table, or connect it to a projector or TV, and the whole ground can follow the match. On iPhones the full-screen button is not available, so cast the page or turn the phone sideways.
If you need a scoreboard for racket sports with games and sets, use the Match Score Keeper. For cricket use the Cricket Scorer.

sections.heading: Kho kho ground size at a glance
paragraphs: A kho kho ground is a rectangle 27 m (88 ft 7 in) long and 16 m (52 ft 5.9 in) wide. The central lane is 0.3 m (11.8 in) wide, each of the 8 cross lanes is 0.35 m (1 ft 1.8 in) wide, and the two poles are 120 to 125 cm high. The diagonal of the ground is 31.38 m (102 ft 11.6 in).

These figures come from the source listed at the end of the guide, and the date they were checked is shown there. The source gives the number and width of the cross lanes but not the spacing between them, so this page does not show it.

sections.heading: How to mark a kho kho ground
paragraphs: Peg out the long sides at 27 m and the ends at 16 m. Measure both diagonals. When they are the same, 31.38 m, the corners are square. Tighten or move a peg until they match.

Then mark the central lane and the cross lanes with chalk or lime, and fix a pole at each end. A school playground or a flat field with a firm, even surface is enough for practice. Keep the area free of stones and holes, because players turn and dive at speed.

sections.heading: Using this page and where the rules differ
paragraphs: Choose Save as image or Save as PDF to take the drawing and the marking plan with you. Everything is made in your browser, and nothing is uploaded.

Rules change by event and level. The number of players in a team, the length of a turn and the clear space around the ground can differ between a school match, a state event and the World Cup, so confirm with the Kho Kho Federation of India or your organiser before you mark a ground for a competition. See also the kabaddi court size page and the full Sports Court and Ground Size Guide.

sections.heading: Kabaddi court size at a glance
paragraphs: A men's kabaddi court is 13 m (42 ft 7.8 in) long and 10 m (32 ft 9.7 in) wide. A women's court is 12 m (39 ft 4.4 in) by 8 m (26 ft 3 in), and a sub-junior court is 11 m (36 ft 1.1 in) by 8 m. A midline splits each court in two, and the diagonals are 16.4 m, 14.42 m and 13.6 m.
The sizes follow the International Kabaddi Federation rules, version 2.1.0. The date they were checked is shown at the end of the guide.

sections.heading: Baulk, bonus and lobby lines
paragraphs: On the men's court the baulk line is 3.75 m (12 ft 3.6 in) from the midline, so 2.75 m (9 ft 0.3 in) from the end line. The bonus line is 1 m beyond the baulk line, 1.75 m (5 ft 8.9 in) from the end line. On the women's and sub-junior courts the baulk line is 3 m (9 ft 10.1 in) from the midline.
A 1 m (3 ft 3.4 in) strip along each long side is the lobby. It becomes part of the court after a touch or struggle starts.

sections.heading: How to mark the court and what space you need
paragraphs: Peg out the outer rectangle, check that both diagonals match, then mark the midline and the baulk, bonus and lobby lines from the marking plan on this page. Choose the version first, because each court has different distances.

The guide lists a desirable ground of 20 m by 20 m and no smaller than 17 m by 18 m around the court. Rules differ by league, so check the current rules of the Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India or your state association. See also the kho kho court size page and the full Sports Court and Ground Size Guide.

sections.heading: Badminton court size at a glance
paragraphs: A badminton court is 13.4 m (43 ft 11.6 in) long and 6.1 m (20 ft 0.2 in) wide for doubles. For singles the court is 5.18 m (16 ft 11.9 in) wide, using the inner side lines. The diagonal is 14.72 m. Line width is 0.04 m (1.6 in).

The net is 1.55 m (5 ft 1 in) high at the posts and 1.524 m (5 ft 0 in) in the middle. The short service line is 1.98 m (6 ft 6 in) from the net, and the long service line for doubles is 0.76 m (2 ft 5.9 in) in from the back line. In singles the back line itself is the long service line.

sections.heading: How to mark a badminton court
paragraphs: Peg out the 13.4 m by 6.1 m rectangle and measure both diagonals. When they match, the corners are square. Mark the net line across the middle, 6.7 m from each back line, then the short service lines 4.72 m from each back line.

Add the centre line 3.05 m from the side line, the long service line for doubles and the singles side lines 0.46 m (1 ft 6.1 in) inside the outer side lines. On a hall floor, use tape in a colour that stands out from the surface, and put the net posts on the doubles side lines.

sections.heading: Space around the court and where rules differ
paragraphs: The guide uses the clear space the BWF asks for in competition halls: 2 m behind the back lines and 1.5 m at the sides, with 9 m of clear height above the court. That makes a space of about 17.4 m x 9.1 m for one court. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to check a room.

School and club halls often squeeze courts closer together, and rules are updated from time to time. Confirm with the Badminton World Federation or your national body before you mark a court for a competition.

sections.heading: Tennis court size at a glance
paragraphs: A tennis court is 23.77 m (77 ft 11.8 in) long and 10.97 m (35 ft 11.9 in) wide for doubles. For singles the court is 8.23 m (27 ft 0 in) wide. The diagonal is 26.18 m.

The service line is 6.4 m (21 ft 0 in) from the net. The net is 1.07 m (3 ft 6.1 in) high at the posts and 0.914 m (3 ft 0 in) in the middle, and the posts stand 0.914 m outside the doubles side lines.

sections.heading: How to mark a tennis court
paragraphs: Peg out the 23.77 m by 10.97 m rectangle and measure both diagonals. When they match, the corners are square. Mark the net line across the middle, 11.885 m from each baseline, then the service lines 6.4 m from the net on both sides.

Add the centre service line, which runs 5.485 m (17 ft 11.9 in) from each side line, and the singles side lines 1.37 m (4 ft 5.9 in) inside the doubles side lines. Most courts are built with doubles lines and the singles lines added inside them.

sections.heading: Space around the court and where rules differ
paragraphs: The ITF recommends at least 5.48 m behind the baselines and 3.05 m at the sides for club and recreational play, and 6.4 m and 3.66 m for international competition. These are minimums. The ITF also recommends a roof height of at least 9 m over the court at the net.

For a home or school court you can plan a tighter fit, but play will feel cramped. Confirm with the International Tennis Federation or your national body for competitions. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to check a plot.

sections.heading: Pickleball court size at a glance
paragraphs: A pickleball court is 13.41 m (44 ft 0 in) long and 6.096 m (20 ft 0 in) wide. The size is the same for singles and doubles. The diagonal is 14.73 m. Lines are 0.051 m (2 in) wide.

The non-volley zone, called the kitchen, is 2.134 m (7 ft 0 in) deep from the net on each side and runs across the full width of the court. The net is 0.914 m (3 ft 0 in) high at the sidelines and 0.864 m (2 ft 10 in) in the middle.

sections.heading: How to mark a pickleball court
paragraphs: Peg out the rectangle and measure both diagonals. The net line sits 6.706 m (22 ft 0 in) from each end line. The kitchen line is 4.572 m (15 ft 0 in) from each end line, and the centre line is 3.048 m (10 ft 0 in) from each side line, running from the kitchen line to the end line.
The size matches a doubles badminton court, so some venues mark both on one floor. A serve that lands on the kitchen line is short and a fault.

sections.heading: Space around the court and where rules differ
paragraphs: USA Pickleball describes a smallest playing area of 9.14 m x 18.29 m (30 ft x 60 ft) and a tournament playing area of 10.36 m x 19.51 m (34 ft x 64 ft). That is a clear space of about 2.44 m (8 ft) behind the end lines and 1.52 m (5 ft) at the sides at the minimum, and 3.05 m (10 ft) and 2.13 m (7 ft) for tournaments.

Rules are updated each year, and school or community courts may differ. Confirm with USA Pickleball or your national body for competitions, and use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to see how many courts fit.

sections.heading: Basketball court size at a glance
paragraphs: A full FIBA basketball court is 28 m (91 ft 10.4 in) long and 15 m (49 ft 2.6 in) wide, measured from the inside edge of the boundary lines. The diagonal is 31.76 m. A 3x3 court is 15 m (49 ft 2.6 in) by 11 m (36 ft 1.1 in).

The rim is 3.05 m (10 ft 0.1 in) above the floor. The free-throw line is 5.8 m (19 ft 0.3 in) from the end line, the lane is 4.9 m (16 ft 0.9 in) wide, the three-point arc has a radius of 6.75 m (22 ft 1.7 in) and the centre circle has a radius of 1.8 m (5 ft 10.9 in).

sections.heading: How to mark a basketball court
paragraphs: Peg out the rectangle and measure both diagonals. Mark the halfway line 14 m (45 ft 11.2 in) from each end line, then the centre circle. At each end mark the free-throw line, the lane, and the free-throw semicircle with a radius of 1.8 m.
The three-point corner lines run 0.9 m (2 ft 11.4 in) in from each side line and meet the arc. The arc is drawn from a point 1.575 m in from the end line.

sections.heading: Space around the court and where rules differ
paragraphs: FIBA asks for obstructions to be at least 2 m from the court, so a full court needs a space of about 32 m x 19 m. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to check a hall or playground.
School, street and league courts are often smaller than a full FIBA court, and other leagues use their own sizes. Confirm with FIBA or your league before you mark a court for competition.

sections.heading: Volleyball court size at a glance
paragraphs: An indoor volleyball court is 18 m (59 ft 0.7 in) long and 9 m (29 ft 6.3 in) wide, split by the net into two 9 m x 9 m halves. A beach court is 16 m (52 ft 5.9 in) by 8 m (26 ft 3 in). The diagonals are 20.12 m and 17.89 m.
The attack line is 3 m (9 ft 10.1 in) from the centre line on an indoor court. The net is 2.43 m (7 ft 11.7 in) high for men and 2.24 m (7 ft 4.2 in) for women.

sections.heading: How to mark a volleyball court
paragraphs: Peg out the rectangle, measure both diagonals and adjust a peg until they match. Mark the centre line across the middle, 9 m from each end line for an indoor court, then the attack lines 3 m on each side of it.
A beach court has no attack line, so only the outer lines and the centre line under the net are marked.

sections.heading: Space around the court and where rules differ
paragraphs: The guide lists a free zone of at least 3 m on all sides as the smallest clear space, and 8 m at the end lines and 5 m at the sidelines for world and official competitions, with at least 7 m of clear height above the court. The figures come from a state guide that cites older rules.
Check the current FIVB or national rules before you build a court for competition. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to see whether a court fits a hall.

sections.heading: Football pitch size at a glance
paragraphs: The Laws of the Game let an 11-a-side pitch be 90 to 120 m long and 45 to 90 m wide, and 100 to 110 m by 64 to 75 m for international matches. A common size is 105 m (344 ft 5.9 in) by 68 m (223 ft 1.2 in), which is a choice and not a rule. Its diagonal is 125.1 m.

The goal is 7.32 m (24 ft 0.2 in) wide inside the posts and the crossbar is 2.44 m (8 ft 0.1 in) high. The goal area reaches 5.5 m (18 ft 0.5 in) from the goal line, the penalty area 16.5 m (54 ft 1.6 in) and the penalty mark is 11 m (36 ft 1.1 in) from the goal line.

sections.heading: How to mark a football pitch
paragraphs: Peg out the touchlines and goal lines and check that both diagonals match. Mark the halfway line across the middle and the centre circle with a radius of 9.15 m (30 ft 0.2 in). At each end, mark the goal area, penalty area, penalty mark and the penalty arc, which has the same 9.15 m radius.
Add a corner arc with a radius of 1 m (3 ft 3.4 in) at each corner.

sections.heading: Space around the pitch and where rules differ
paragraphs: The Laws give ranges and not one size, and youth and local pitches often differ. The guide does not list a run-off area, because the Laws do not set one. Upright advertising must be at least 1 m from the touchlines and the goal net.
Check the rules of your league, school or federation before you mark a pitch. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to see which pitch size fits a ground.

sections.heading: Cricket pitch and ground size at a glance
paragraphs: A cricket pitch is 22 yards, which is 20.12 m (66 ft 0 in), long and 10 ft (3.048 m) wide. The diagonal of the pitch is 20.35 m. The centre line is 1.524 m (5 ft 0 in) from each side.

The ground is not fixed. International boundaries for men are 65 to 90 yards from the centre of the pitch, which is 59.44 m (195 ft 0 in) to 82.3 m (270 ft 0 in). For women's international matches the range is 60 to 70 yards, which is 54.86 m (180 ft 0 in) to 64.01 m (210 ft 0 in).

sections.heading: How to mark a cricket pitch and ground
paragraphs: Mark the pitch first, as a rectangle 20.12 m long and 3.048 m wide, with the centre line along the length. Then choose a boundary distance and measure it from the middle of the pitch in every direction. Real grounds are ovals, and the guide draws a circle with the boundary distance as its radius, which is the safest size to plan for.

For limited-overs matches the fielding circle has a radius of 27.43 m (90 ft 0 in) from each wicket, joined by straight lines. The guide shows the straight part, which is 32 m (105 ft 0 in) at the smallest men's boundary.

sections.heading: Space around the ground and where rules differ
paragraphs: The guide keeps a gap of at least 3 yards, 2.74 m (9 ft 0 in), between the boundary rope and fencing or advertising boards. School, club and local grounds use their own limits and are often much smaller than international grounds.
Check the rules of your association or the ICC before you mark a ground for a match. See also the Cricket Scorer and the Cricket Run Rate Calculator for scoring.

sections.heading: Hockey pitch size at a glance
paragraphs: A field hockey pitch is 91.4 m (299 ft 10.4 in) long and 55 m (180 ft 5.4 in) wide, which is 100 yards by 60 yards. The diagonal is 106.67 m. Lines are 0.075 m (3 in) wide.

Each goal is 3.66 m (12 ft 0.1 in) wide and 2.14 m (7 ft 0.3 in) high. The shooting circle has a radius of 14.63 m (48 ft 0 in), the 23 m line is 22.9 m (75 ft 1.6 in) from the back line and the penalty spot is 6.475 m (21 ft 2.9 in) from the goal line.

sections.heading: How to mark a hockey pitch
paragraphs: Peg out the rectangle and check that both diagonals match. Mark the halfway line 45.7 m (149 ft 11.2 in) from each back line and the 23 m lines 22.9 m from each back line.
The shooting circle is drawn from two quadrant arcs of 14.63 m radius centred on the goalposts, joined by a 3.66 m straight line. Mark the penalty spot 6.475 m from the goal line.

sections.heading: Space around the pitch and where rules differ
paragraphs: The FIH asks for run-off of at least 2 m at the side lines and 3 m at the back lines, so a full pitch needs a space of about 97.4 m x 59 m. The run-off is a minimum, and the last metre can be a different surface.

School and club pitches are often smaller. Confirm the size with the International Hockey Federation or your national body before you mark a pitch for competition. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to check a ground.

sections.heading: Table tennis table size at a glance
paragraphs: A table tennis table is 2.74 m (8 ft 11.9 in) long, 1.525 m (5 ft 0 in) wide and 0.76 m (2 ft 5.9 in) above the floor. The net is 0.152 m (6 in) above the playing surface and runs across the middle of the table, 1.37 m (4 ft 5.9 in) from each end.
A line down the centre of the table, 0.762 m (2 ft 6 in) from each side, divides it for doubles serves.

sections.heading: Playing space for table tennis
paragraphs: The competition playing space is 14 m (45 ft 11.2 in) long and 7 m (22 ft 11.6 in) wide, with 5 m of clear height. Reduced spaces are allowed for masters events, 10 m (32 ft 9.7 in) by 5 m (16 ft 4.9 in), and for wheelchair events, 8 m (26 ft 3 in) by 6 m (19 ft 8.2 in).
The 14 m x 7 m x 5 m space is the competition minimum. Home and club tables need much less. The rules do not set a recreational size, so leave enough room to step back from the table.

sections.heading: Choosing a room and where rules differ
paragraphs: For a home table, measure the room first and leave space around all four sides. Players need room to step back from the table, so check both the length and the width of the room.

Confirm the sizes with the International Table Tennis Federation or your national body before you set up a space for a competition. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to check a room.

sections.heading: Squash court size at a glance
paragraphs: A singles squash court is 9.75 m (31 ft 11.9 in) long and 6.4 m (21 ft 0 in) wide, enclosed by four walls. A doubles court is 13.72 m (45 ft 0.2 in) long and 7.62 m (25 ft 0 in) wide.

On a singles court the front wall top line is 4.57 m (14 ft 11.9 in) high, the back wall top line is 2.13 m (6 ft 11.9 in) high, the tin is 0.48 m (1 ft 6.9 in) high and the service line on the front wall is 1.78 m (5 ft 10.1 in) high. On a doubles court the front wall top line is 6.09 m (19 ft 11.8 in) high.

sections.heading: Squash court markings and walls
paragraphs: A squash court is built with walls, so most of the numbers on the page are heights on the walls and not distances on the floor. The floor lines include the short line and the half-court line, and the guide does not draw them because the two sources we checked differed slightly on the short line position.
The tin is a strip across the bottom of the front wall, and a ball that hits it is out.

sections.heading: Planning a court and where rules differ
paragraphs: A squash court is a building project, with a floor, four walls and a roof, and you should have a qualified person check the plan. This guide is for planning and is not an engineering approval.
Confirm the sizes with World Squash or your national body before you build. Use the Fit my space tab on the Sports Court and Ground Size Guide to see whether a court fits a building.

sections.heading: Round robin for 4 teams at a glance
paragraphs: In a round robin with 4 teams, every team plays every other team once. That is 4 x 3 ÷ 2 = 6 matches, and each team plays 3 of them. The matches are shared out in 3 rounds of 2 matches.
Because 4 is an even number, every team plays in every round. You need 2 courts or pitches to play a whole round at the same time.

sections.heading: Knockout bracket for 6 teams at a glance
paragraphs: A knockout with 6 teams has 5 matches, because every match knocks out one team and only the champion is left. The bracket is built on 8 places and has 3 rounds: Quarter-finals (4 matches), Semi-finals (2 matches), Final (1 match).
6 is not a power of 2, so 2 places are left empty. The top 2 seeds get a bye, which means going straight to the next round without playing, and the other 4 teams play 2 matches in the first round.

sections.heading: First round for 6 teams
paragraphs: This is the first round the tool makes for 6 teams, in seed order. Team 1 is the top seed. Replace the team names with your own.
Team 1 has a bye, Team 4 vs Team 5, Team 2 has a bye, Team 3 vs Team 6.
The slot order for 8 places is 1, 8, 4, 5, 2, 7, 3, 6. Seed 1 plays the lowest seed, and the top seeds are kept apart until the latest round possible.

sections.heading: Running the knockout
paragraphs: Play each round in turn. Rounds get shorter: 4 matches, 2 matches, 1 match. With one court, that is 5 matches in all.
The tool does not make a third place match. If you want one, add a match between the two losing semi-finalists before the final.
